title: Adyar Breaks the Nawab's Line
subtitle: When the Adyar Ran Shallow, Empire Ran Deep
region: San Thome and the Adyar River, Madras/Chennai
moral: The future sometimes announces itself first as a tactical surprise.

sources.citation: French Compagnie des Indes correspondence of Joseph Francois Dupleix and Madras/Pondicherry records, 1746
sources.note: Contemporary administrative record from the French side around the capture and retention of Madras.

sources.citation: Ananda Ranga Pillai, Private Diary, entries for the Dupleix period, 1746
sources.note: Contemporary Pondicherry diary by Dupleix's dubash, valuable for French-Carnatic politics and local reporting.

sources.citation: Robert Orme, A History of the Military Transactions of the British Nation in Indostan, Vol. I (1763)
sources.note: Early British East India Company-side narrative, close to participants but not neutral.

sources.citation: G.B. Malleson, History of the French in India (1868); P.J. Marshall, ed., The Eighteenth Century in Indian History (2003)
sources.note: Later military and scholarly treatments of the Carnatic Wars and the company-state shift.

dialogue.text: In October 1746, near the Adyar’s shallow bends, Louis Paradis and Mahfuz Khan fought a brief, sharp action that showed all of India how companies could humble kingdoms.
The First Carnatic War began far from the Adyar, as Europe’s War of the Austrian Succession spilled onto the Coromandel coast, dragging Madras and Pondicherry into a quarrel not their own.

panels.shot: medium shot inside European-style council chamber

dialogue.text: Madras, held by the English Company, was a busy trade town under the distant suzerainty of Nawab Anwaruddin Khan of Arcot, who saw Europeans as mere merchants owing him deference and tribute.

panels.shot: naval wide shot from sea level

dialogue.text: In September 1746, Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais brought a French fleet before Madras, and after bombardment and negotiation, Fort St George surrendered to the Compagnie des Indes.

panels.shot: interior wide in Pondicherry council hall

dialogue.text: La Bourdonnais treated Madras as a prize to ransom, but Governor Dupleix saw more. If he kept the fort, he could weaken the English and lift the French Company to a new, territorial power.
Yet by long practice, the Nawab claimed a say in European wars along his coast. He expected Madras to pass to his authority, not remain in foreign hands behind foreign guns.
When Dupleix refused to hand over Fort St George, Nawab Anwaruddin sent his son Mahfuz Khan with a large Carnatic force; to meet him, Dupleix relied on a quieter man, Major Louis Paradis.
Orme and the company records speak of perhaps nine to eleven hundred men, Europeans and Indian sepoys, drilled together in French fashion, moving north towards the Adyar in October 1746.
Across the river, Mahfuz Khan’s army ran into the thousands. Exact numbers differ in the records, but all agree his host dwarfed Paradis’s column in horses, men and banners.
Between them ran the Adyar, not yet the broad city river of later centuries but a changing stream with fords and sandbanks. Here, on 24 October, both sides tested more than the water.

dialogue.speaker: louis_paradis_and_mahfuz_khan
dialogue.text: “Press them to the water and they will yield,” Mahfuz Khan states calmly.

panels.shot: tight medium on Paradis and sepoys forming ranks

dialogue.text: Paradis could not match numbers, so he trusted discipline. His letters speak of fire control, close order and the confidence of men who knew their places in line and in battle.
Instead of waiting to be overwhelmed, Paradis chose to cross. In close, controlled order, his mixed European and Indian force stepped into the river, trusting drill against a larger foe.

When the line touched firm ground, Paradis ordered his men to fire by platoon. Orme notes the effect of synchronized volleys, each rank stepping, firing and falling back to reload with drilled precision.

panels.shot: three-quarter view of light artillery firing

dialogue.text: Behind the muskets, small cannon spoke in turn. French records and later histories emphasize how well-handled artillery, sighted low, shook cavalry used to looser patterns of fire.
Then came the bayonets. At Paradis’s word, his front ranks advanced with cold steel, still in line. It was not ferocity alone, but cohesion under command, that pressed into the Nawab’s formations.

panels.shot: wide shot of Carnatic line breaking

dialogue.text: The sources speak of a rout, not a slaughter. Under the sustained volleys and advance, segments of the Carnatic line gave way, their withdrawal uncoordinated as Paradis’s smaller force held together.

panels.shot: medium on Mahfuz Khan in retreat

dialogue.speaker: louis_paradis_and_mahfuz_khan
dialogue.text: “Strength in powder and drill,” he notes inwardly, “not in splendour alone.”
For the French, this was no conquest of the Carnatic, but a hard proof. A few hundred cohesive troops, European and Indian together, had stood and advanced against several times their number.

panels.shot: interior shot of Ananda Ranga Pillai writing

dialogue.text: Ananda Ranga Pillai noted the political shock. The Nawab, who had treated companies as petitioners, now saw they could fight as disciplined armies, a lesson his successors would not forget.

Madras itself would return to the English in 1748 under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, yet the memory of Adyar endured, guiding both French and British as they raised sepoy battalions and bargained with Indian courts.

panels.shot: closing contemplative wide of quiet Adyar

dialogue.text: At Adyar, the future of India’s wars stepped through shallow water: not a clash of races, but a contest of organization and arms, where a tactical surprise announced the age of the company-state.
